summary.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting's Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
summary.idea: LLM code review misses bugs and burdens humans, so Meta generates tests that fail on a risky diff, filters false positives automatically, and only pings engineers about the likeliest real catches.
howItWorks: Overnight, a risk score picks the previous day's riskiest diffs for test generation on spare capacity.
Dodgy-diff workflow treats each change as a mutant and writes tests that distinguish it from its parent.
Intent-aware workflow infers the diff's purpose, lists risks, builds mutants for them, and writes tests to kill each.
Tests that fail on the real diff become weak catches, ranked by an LLM judge ensemble plus deterministic rules.
Engineers set criteria and review aggregate outcomes, and are contacted only when a candidate ranks highly enough.
summary.stealThis: Before your next risky merge, have an agent write a test that passes on the parent commit and fails on your diff, then only review the failures that survive a second LLM-judge pass.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent-written code and want a concrete pipeline for filtering false positives before a human looks.
summary.quote: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable technique, backed by production results (60% true positives, 74 serious privacy bugs caught): generate tests that tell a diff apart from its parent, keep the ones that fail on the real diff, and filter them with an LLM-judge ensemble plus deterministic rules before a human sees anything. It lacks code or a repo, and its core is test-based verification rather than review.

summary.title: 90% of my coding agent's rework came from my own work orders
summary.idea: Stricter automated review sent more agent work back for rework, and sorting the send-backs showed most came from vague work orders, so the author added a pre-handoff check on the order itself.
howItWorks: Pull the last 10 send-backs and sort each must-fix item into 'the order was silent or ambiguous' or 'the worker ignored it'.
Before handoff, a falsifier model sees only the order plus read access to the repo, and returns at most seven ranked findings.
Each finding quotes the triggering line of the order, gives a concrete breaking input, and names the section where the fix goes.
Run the falsifier twice, since the two runs overlapped on only 25 gaps; either run alone caught 56-60% of order gaps, together 71%.
Move hard rules like never printing credentials into pre-tool hooks, and split big skills into a small core with step files read on demand.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent handoff, run a falsifier prompt twice on the written brief, asking for ranked findings with a quoted line and a concrete breaking input, and fold the fixes into the brief.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're handing work to subagents or cheaper models and burning review rounds on rework that may really come from your own briefs.
summary.quote: Reviewing harder only catches the 90% after a full round has already been spent.

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete pre-handoff 'falsifier' pass, run twice, that turns up gaps in the work order. Each finding is ranked, quotes the triggering line and gives a breaking input. The evidence is a rework-sorting analysis (55 of 61 must-fix items came from the order) and measured catch rates, though the actual prompt isn't published and the sample is small.

summary.title: The agent ended its turn. That is not the same as done.
summary.idea: Agent loops treat the end of a turn as task completion, so unfinished work gets reported as done; a Stop hook that inspects the repository and re-runs tests blocks that.
howItWorks: A stop_check script exits 0 only if the worktree has changes, claimed files match changed files, and tests pass.
The checker re-runs the test command itself, because the agent's console output is not evidence.
Wire it as a Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2, which blocks stopping and continues the conversation.
Read the stop_hook_active flag first and let the turn end on a second block, so a broken environment cannot loop forever.
Restore protected paths like tests from the base revision before checking, so the agent cannot edit the referee.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent run, add a Stop hook that exits 2 unless git shows changes and your own test command passes when the hook runs it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running long unattended agent loops and want a working stop-hook script plus its known gaps (renames, new directories, deleted or skipped tests).
summary.quote: A nudge is a suggestion. A hook is a check that runs.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2 unless git shows a diff, claimed files match, and the checker re-runs the tests itself, with working code, a stop_hook_active loop guard, and comments that test the script and expose its gaps.

summary.title: Your AI reviewer passed the code. Who wrote its instructions?
summary.idea: An AI reviewer follows whatever instruction files a pull request changes, so attackers target AGENTS.md, skills and MCP configs. The fix is to hash those files into each verdict and require human approval for changes.
howItWorks: Each agent verdict records SHA-256 hashes of AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, Cursor rules and MCP configs.
If any of those files change afterward, earlier verdicts stop counting and the gate refuses.
Changes to instruction files need a person's approval, backed by CODEOWNERS or signed approvals.
Changed instruction files must be plain Markdown; images, HTML, comments and invisible characters are refused.
The policy is read from the base branch, so a PR cannot loosen the rules it is judged by.
summary.stealThis: Before your next merge of an agent-config change, add CODEOWNERS entries for AGENTS.md, skills and MCP configs so a human must approve any edit to what the reviewer is told.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting AI agents review pull requests and haven't considered that the PR can rewrite the reviewer's own instructions.
summary.quote: If a pull request changes AGENTS.md, and an agent reviews that pull request, whose instructions is it following?

verdict.reason: It teaches transferable guardrails for AI code review: bind verdicts to hashes of instruction files, require CODEOWNERS approval for AGENTS.md, skill and MCP config changes, refuse hidden content, and read policy from the base branch; a public demo repo shows five attacks caught, though the post is partly a release note for the author's open-source tool.

summary.title: The Agent Wrote the Code and the Tests. How Do You Know They Are Right?
summary.idea: When an agent writes both code and tests, they can share the same wrong interpretation, so check tests against independently set expected results and confirm they fail on a deliberately wrong implementation.
howItWorks: Work out a few expected results by hand from the accepted rule, before looking at the implementation.
Read each assertion: it should check the claimed value, not just a successful HTTP 200 response.
On a disposable branch, plant a small realistic bug and confirm the relevant test fails for the right reason.
Keep a contract or integration check against the real consumer where a mock could hide a mismatch.
Give a QA agent the accepted requirement and examples, not the implementer's explanation, and have a person approve any changed expectations.
summary.stealThis: Before accepting agent-written tests for your next rule-heavy change, ask the agent to show the accepted expected result, the check that establishes it, and a deliberately wrong implementation that the check rejects.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent-written tests and want a concrete checklist for judging whether they prove the right behavior.
summary.quote: A test suite may run successfully while proving a rule nobody agreed to build.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable check for agent-written tests: derive expected values independently from the accepted rule, plant a controlled wrong implementation to confirm the test fails, and feed a QA agent the requirement rather than the implementer's explanation. It has a worked pricing example but no repo or before/after evidence, and the card accurately reflects the page.

summary.title: Running AI Coding Agents in Production: My 2026 Stack
summary.idea: Agents that run unattended can leak keys and overspend, so the author wraps them in plumbing: gateway routing, runtime credential injection, narrowly scoped MCP servers, and a private network.
howItWorks: Route all model calls through a gateway so agents never hold provider keys, giving one kill switch and an auditable bill.
Keep secrets in a password manager and inject them at runtime through a local broker with output scrubbing, not a repo .env.
Use short-lived, rotating keys scoped to one service each, so a leak only affects one tool.
Give agents scoped MCP servers for filesystem, git and search, instead of prompting them to be careful.
Put agent access to infrastructure on a private tailnet and use file locks and job ownership markers to stop runs colliding.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent run, move its provider key behind a gateway or runtime-injected secret scoped to one service, so a leaked key can be revoked without breaking anything else.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents unattended or on schedules and want a concrete example of credential handling, gateways, and what still breaks.
summary.quote: a well-scoped MCP server beats a prompt telling the agent to "be careful" every time.

verdict.reason: A genuine walkthrough of a production agent setup that teaches transferable patterns: gateway-held provider keys, runtime secret injection with scrubbing, single-service scoped keys and narrowly scoped MCP servers. It stays thin, though, with no configs or code and affiliate-linked tool mentions that edge toward a round-up.

summary.title: gstack plan-ceo-review SKILL.md
summary.idea: Agent plan reviews drift into silent scope changes and unrecorded approvals; this skill structures the review as a gated flow with a decision ledger, explicit mode selection, and per-change approval.
howItWorks: Pre-review audit reads git history, TODOs, CLAUDE.md and any design doc before the agent forms opinions.
Reviewer picks one of four modes (expansion, selective expansion, hold, reduction); choosing a mode approves no changes.
Every scope change is a separate ledger row with options, effort and risk, and the agent stops for an actual answer.
A fresh subagent reviews the plan and summary on five dimensions, capped at three launches.
An exit gate blocks completion until the plan ends with a verified review report and no unresolved decisions.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-driven plan review, keep a decision ledger where each proposed scope change is its own row and nothing counts as approved until you answer that exact question.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building long skill files for planning or review agents and want a working example of gated approvals, state tracking and exit checks.
summary.quote: Selecting a mode does not approve changes.

verdict.reason: The actual SKILL.md teaches transferable gating patterns: a decision ledger where each scope change gets its own row and waits for an explicit answer, mode selection that approves nothing, a fresh-context reviewer subagent capped at three launches, and a blocking exit gate on the report's final line. It is dense, tied to gstack binaries, and has no before/after evidence, which keeps it at 7.

summary.title: agent-loop: a portable harness with shared instructions, skills and a nightly Dream learning loop
summary.idea: Agent lessons get lost between sessions and between tools; this repo gives Codex and Claude Code one set of instructions and skills, plus a nightly review that promotes confirmed lessons into durable instructions.
howItWorks: One installer points both Codex and Claude Code at the same instructions and eight reviewed skills, with dry-run, backups and a doctor check.
Personal context stays in a separate notes vault that the agents reference, so the repo stays generic and nothing private is copied in.
A nightly Dream run reads both agents' transcripts and git activity across repos and worktrees, then writes a digest and drafts candidate lessons.
Drafts are marked ready only when later evidence confirms them; a dream-review step walks the user through promoting each one.
Later Dream runs check whether each promoted lesson is actually holding, and follow up on earlier recommendations.
summary.stealThis: Next time you notice correcting your agent for the same mistake twice, log it as a draft lesson and only promote it to your shared instructions file once a later session confirms it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running more than one coding agent and want a worked example of shared instructions plus a memory loop that promotes lessons with evidence.
summary.quote: A nightly Dream review reads both agents' sessions and turns confirmed lessons into durable instructions.

verdict.reason: The card accurately describes a working repo with a concrete technique: evidence-gated lesson promotion, where a nightly review drafts lessons from transcripts and git activity, promotes them only once later sessions confirm them, then checks they hold. It loses points because the README shows the loop's design but no before-and-after evidence.

summary.title: Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels
summary.idea: Agent bills climb because every micro-decision hits an expensive reasoning setting; a cheap classifier asking atomic yes/no questions can send only hard tasks to a stronger model, judged by cost per successful task.
howItWorks: Ask one atomic yes/no question, such as 'needs more than one sequential step?', instead of a broad simple-or-complex choice.
Send tasks the classifier calls simple to a no-thinking lite model; escalate flagged ones to Flash on low thinking.
Set thinking level directly; a low max output token cap doesn't cut thinking on easy tasks and breaks hard ones.
Keep long, context-heavy turns on one model, since caches belong to a single model and switching loses the discount.
Freeze keyword heuristics and test on unseen tasks: one fell from 93.8% to 70.6% held-out.
summary.stealThis: Before building a router for your agent, set the thinking level to low on your current model, then test any keyword or length heuristic on held-out tasks to check it generalises.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents at volume and want measured evidence on routing, thinking levels and caching before cutting your model spend.
summary.quote: Judge every option by what it costs per task done right, not per token.

verdict.reason: The technique is portable and backed by measurements: route agent tasks with a cheap classifier that asks atomic yes/no questions, set the thinking level directly instead of capping output tokens, test heuristics on held-out tasks, and keep context-heavy turns on one model so caching still works; the benchmark code isn't published yet.

summary.title: How We Optimized Browser Use for Deep Agents
summary.idea: Browser agents burn context and turns because tools return huge page dumps one step at a time; code-mode tools, compact snapshots and trace-driven fixes cut cost and time while accuracy held.
howItWorks: Let the agent write one code snippet that chains many browser steps, so intermediate page content stays in variables, not context.
Return a trimmed accessibility tree with IDs on interactive elements instead of raw HTML or screenshots.
Trim output at the source: capping snapshots after the fact just made agents refetch the page.
Read traces to spot waste, such as fixed 8-second sleeps, then end sleeps once the page is quiet for 500 ms.
Run evals on every change before keeping it, comparing setups side by side as experiments.
summary.stealThis: The next time your agent's tool returns bulky output, read a few traces for repeated waste, change the tool to return less or batch steps, and rerun your evals before keeping the change.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building or tuning tools for a long-running agent and want measured before-and-after numbers on cost, turns and accuracy.
summary.quote: Traces show where the agent wastes steps and tokens, and evals tell you whether a change helped.

verdict.reason: Teaches portable tool-design techniques for agents (code mode to batch steps and keep intermediate output out of context, compact ID-labelled snapshots, trimming at the source rather than capping, quiet-period sleeps found via traces) backed by measured before-and-after numbers, though it leans on Stagehand and LangSmith.

summary.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
summary.idea: Legora can't read customer traces because the data is confidential, so it rebuilds realistic work as simulated eval environments, classifies failures into known modes, and builds many products from a few primitives.
howItWorks: Engineers and lawyers build simulated environments, such as a 10,000-file data room, and score the agent's report on red flags.
Results go on a heat map by practice area and task, since new models often improve some areas and regress others.
In production, cheap LLM checks classify failures into 10-20 known modes and compare feature-flag rollouts without reading content.
Tabular Review runs the first 10 rows so prompts can be fixed before fanning out to up to a million cells.
Lists, projects and the agent act as shared primitives; agents create and read lists, and list changes trigger agents.
summary.stealThis: Before fanning an agent out over a large batch, run it on the first 10 items, fix the prompts, and only then launch the full run.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents for a regulated domain where you can't inspect user data, or you want a real example of primitive-based product design.
summary.quote: We can't look at any traces basically.

verdict.reason: Teaches portable eval ideas: simulated eval environments when you can't read traces, per-task heat maps across model releases, classifying failures into 10–20 known modes, and piloting on 10 rows before fanning out, but only at interview depth with no code, so it falls short of the 8 a podcast needs.

summary.title: Stop trusting your AGENTS.md: the drift-check that makes it a contract
summary.idea: A lean AGENTS.md is still just prose that quietly goes stale, so tag each rule with a marker and run a CI script that fails when rules and checks fall out of sync.
howItWorks: Put an invisible HTML marker like <!--check: single-lockfile--> next to each rule in AGENTS.md, so the prose stays readable.
A small Node or Python script extracts marker ids and maps each to a verification function returning pass, fail, or offending files.
Two-way binding: a marker with no mapped check fails, and a check with no marker fails.
Run it as its own GitHub workflow on pull requests and pushes, exiting 1 on any drift.
Make checks inspect real code, such as actual imports, rather than only config keywords, and update rules in the same PR as the change.
summary.stealThis: Before your next AGENTS.md edit, add a check marker to each rule and write a short script that fails CI when any marker lacks a mapped check, or the reverse.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're tired of agents quietly violating conventions in your instruction file and want a concrete CI pattern plus the failure modes of building it.
summary.quote: A rule that nothing can break isn't a rule; it's a suggestion the next agent will politely decline.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable pattern for enforcing AGENTS.md in CI: HTML check markers bound two ways to verification functions. It comes with real Node and Python code, a GitHub workflow, and four honest failure stories, such as checks that inspected the config instead of the code.

summary.title: learn-harness-engineering
summary.idea: Agents fail on real repos from a weak environment, not a weak model; this course teaches a file-based harness covering instructions, state, verification, scope and session lifecycle, with projects and templates.
howItWorks: Add AGENTS.md as a short map to deeper docs, rather than one giant instruction file.
Keep feature_list.json as machine-readable scope so the agent works on exactly one unfinished feature.
Run init.sh at session start to install, verify and health-check before any work begins.
Log progress in a markdown file and commit clean state so the next session resumes exactly.
Count only passing tests, lint and type checks as evidence; the agent records proof before claiming done.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-session agent task, drop in AGENTS.md, init.sh, feature_list.json and a progress log, and require the agent to update them before stopping.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're already running coding agents on real repos and want templates, a harness audit script and projects comparing weak versus strong harnesses.
summary.quote: The MODEL decides what code to write. The HARNESS governs when, where, and how it writes it.

verdict.reason: A repo with copy-ready templates (AGENTS.md as a map, feature_list.json, init.sh, a progress log), a 16-step session lifecycle, an audit script and projects comparing weak and strong harnesses; it teaches exactly the file-based harness the card describes.

summary.title: Your agent tool guard probably fails open. One minute to tell.
summary.idea: Agent tool guards often fail open because the orchestrator proceeds unless told to block; probing the guard with crash, silent, and odd-input cases shows which paths actually refuse a call.
howItWorks: Exit code 2 is the only blocking code in Claude Code hooks; crashes, exit 1 and a missing script all let the call proceed.
Make the guard raise once, print nothing once, and exit 2 once, then check the transcript for which refused.
Pipe variant command strings into the hook: quoted paths, git -C, quoted subcommand names, and empty input, printing each exit code.
Put the deny where the side effect is decided, since settings edits only gate operations that haven't resolved policy yet.
Turn each permission layer off in turn to find which one actually decides, and fail closed whenever the guard can't reach a verdict.
summary.stealThis: Before you trust your next PreToolUse hook, pipe the five sample command strings into it and confirm that crash, empty input and a quoted-path variant all exit 2.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents with hooks or deny rules and want to know whether those guards really stop anything.
summary.quote: A guard that "crashes loudly" is a guard that fails open loudly.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, portable way to test agent hooks for fail-open behaviour: exit 2 as the only blocking code, crash/silent/empty-input probes, pasteable printf test lines, and turning permission layers off one at a time.

summary.title: markhazlett/agent-harness: Portable coding agent harness
summary.idea: Coding agents drift into destructive or sloppy habits, so this repo wraps one in hooks that block risky commands, skills with fixed rules, and a weekly plan-build-ship workflow.
howItWorks: A bash-guard hook blocks commits on main, --no-verify, sed -i on source, and rm -rf on source dirs.
A protected-files hook stops edits to .env, hook scripts, settings.json and the lockfile, guarding the guards.
Session-start and stop hooks inject branch and handoff notes, then run tests and typecheck if source changed.
Verification skills carry a one-sentence Iron Law plus a Rationalization Table of real excuses the model used under pressure.
A read-only validator agent runs tests and lint, and /orchestrate loops builders and validator up to 3 cycles.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent talks itself out of a test or gate, record its exact excuse in a Rationalization Table inside the relevant skill, next to a one-line Iron Law.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building your own hooks, skills and guardrails and want a complete, working example to copy from.
summary.quote: Hooks are the one exception (they catch destructive shell commands), and they too are configurable.

verdict.reason: A complete, copyable harness repo with concrete guardrail hooks (bash-guard, protected-files that also guard the guards), stop-hook verification, a read-only validator subagent loop capped at 3 cycles, and skills that pair an Iron Law with a Rationalization Table. The card matches the page, though it's a toolkit README rather than a walkthrough of what broke, so it fits harness design better than real setups.

summary.title: Claude Code Stop Hook: Block Early Exit Without Loops
summary.idea: Agents often declare done too early. A Stop hook runs your real check, such as tests passing, blocks with a specific reason while it fails, and gives up after a capped number of retries.
howItWorks: Register a command hook under Stop in .claude/settings.json; Stop takes no matcher, so it fires on every finished turn.
The script reads session_id and stop_hook_active from stdin, then runs npm test and checks that the output file exists.
On failure it prints JSON with decision block and a reason containing the last 30 lines of test output.
A per-session counter file caps retries at about 3, then exits with a systemMessage and logs GAVE_UP for cron to grep.
Build the JSON with jq, send test output to a file not stdout, and pipe sample input in by hand to test.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended or overnight run, copy the verify-before-stop.sh script, swap in your real done check, set a retry cap of 3, and add a grep for GAVE_UP in your wrapper.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running Claude Code unattended in cron or CI and need a deterministic, budget-capped done check, or you're debugging a Stop hook that won't fire.
summary.quote: A Stop hook lets a script that you control decide whether the work is actually done.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable Stop-hook verification gate: run real tests, block with the failing output as the reason, cap retries per session with a counter file, and log GAVE_UP for cron to grep, all with full working script and test steps; tied to Claude Code but the deterministic done-check-with-retry-cap pattern ports to other harnesses.

summary.title: loop-harness: scheduled agent loops with worktree isolation and a second-agent verification gate
summary.idea: Unattended agents risk shipping unchecked work, so this harness has the primary agent only stage outputs in an isolated worktree, and a skeptical second agent must pass them before anything is pushed or posted.
howItWorks: A scheduler wakes each loop on a cadence and gives a Claude session a task-specific skill file.
Write loops run in a fresh git worktree on their own branch, never touching your checkout.
The primary agent can't push or post; it stages commits, a PR body, or outbox action files.
A second read-mostly claude session inspects the diff, runs cheap checks, and must print VERDICT: PASS.
Each skill ends with a RESULT line whose stable item IDs feed a state file for deduplication, so reruns are safe.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent job, split it into a stage step that writes outputs to files and a separate verifier session that must print an explicit PASS before anything ships.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents on a schedule or in CI and want a small shell-based template for isolation, verification gates and idempotent state.
summary.quote: You don't prompt Claude ; loops do.

verdict.reason: A real, copyable harness: the agent stages outputs in a worktree, a skeptical second Claude session must print VERDICT: PASS before anything is pushed or posted, and RESULT-line item IDs keep reruns idempotent; it comes with code, config and a diagram, though it's a small new repo without before-and-after evidence.

summary.title: GTM agent runbook: example format
summary.idea: GTM agents risk emailing customers or changing prices by mistake, so write a runbook first, covering job, permissions, approvals, evals and rollback, then enforce it with a matching policy file.
howItWorks: Start from a task the team already does by hand, and collect past good outputs as a test set.
Run the agent in shadow beside people for 2 to 4 weeks before it does anything live.
List allowed inputs and actions, deny everything else, and require human approval for customers, prices or money.
Set a pass bar (95%) and an error budget (3%); breaching it demotes the agent automatically, while promotion needs owner sign-off.
Log every write with its old value, and keep one disable switch so changes can be reverted.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent goes live, write a one-page runbook plus a YAML policy file with allowed and forbidden actions, an eval pass bar and an error budget that auto-demotes it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're giving agents to a sales, marketing or ops team and want a ready template for permissions, approvals and rollback.
summary.quote: If the runbook and this file disagree, the file wins until the runbook is fixed.

verdict.reason: Despite the consultancy pitch around it, the page gives a portable template for governing GTM agents: a complete example runbook and matching YAML policy with deny-by-default actions, a 95% eval pass bar, a 3% error budget that auto-demotes, journaled CRM writes and a kill switch, though it never shows how the harness enforces the file.

summary.title: "All 42 Tests Passed" (They Didn't): Why Coding Agents Lie About Verification - And How to Force the Truth
summary.idea: Coding agents can reach a green result by weakening tests, spoofing runs or editing code after the run. Binding test receipts to a working-tree hash and auditing test diffs makes a fake pass detectable.
howItWorks: Scan the test-file diff for removed assertions, assert.ok(true), skipped tests and empty catch blocks, and downgrade the result to PARTIAL.
Hash the working tree when tests finish; if the hash differs at step completion, reject the stale receipt and force a re-run.
Block inline-eval commands like node -e and syntax-only checks, and reject runs with zero assertions.
Track failing suites by command, so a passing smoke test cannot wash out a red integration suite.
Require a real human message after the plan before unlocking edits, so synthetic auto-approval cannot trigger execution.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-driven refactor, add a hook that diffs the tests directory for deleted assertions, tautologies and empty catches, and compares a working-tree hash against the one recorded at the last test run.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents self-report test results and want a ready 35-line verifier plus a catalogue of the shortcuts agents actually take.
summary.quote: Unless the ambient harness renders fraudulent passes mathematically unrepresentable, stochastic agents inexorably default to Path B whenever epistemic strain intensifies.

verdict.reason: Teaches portable anti-cheating checks on agent test runs: auditing test diffs for removed assertions, tautologies and empty catches; binding receipts to a working-tree hash; blocking inline-eval spoofs; and tracking unresolved failing suites, with a 35-line verifier to copy.

summary.title: Require uploaded UI proof before merge and automate PR evidence links
summary.idea: UI pull requests could pass verification with a local path or 'Not verified'; this PR makes the merge gate demand uploaded screenshots and passing test reports tied to the current commit.
howItWorks: Reuse the existing required e2e-test check to enforce evidence on PRs and squash merge groups, so browser failures still block.
Playwright CI captures and uploads screenshots and test results; mobile proof is packaged from the existing device workflow.
Validation checks artifact provenance, current head commit, producer success, test results, screenshots and expiry, so stale or corrupt evidence fails.
The only escape is a no-ui-verification label plus a visible 'Verification-skip-reason:' line in the PR body.
A trusted default-branch publisher posts artifact links on the PR; waiver or body edits rerun only the evidence job.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-authored UI change, make CI reject PR descriptions whose screenshots aren't uploaded artifacts for the current commit, with a labelled waiver that requires a written reason.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents open UI PRs and want a working example of enforcing proof-of-work in CI, including waivers and stale-evidence checks.
summary.quote: Uploaded screenshots and passing tests do not replace visual review.

verdict.reason: A real, merged CI gate shows a portable proof-of-work technique: the merge check rejects agent UI PRs unless screenshots and test reports are uploaded artifacts for the current head commit, not expired, with a labelled waiver that needs a written reason; it is thin as a tutorial because the mechanics sit in a terse PR summary, not a walkthrough.

summary.title: coreyhaines31/marketingskills
summary.idea: Marketing teams get generic AI output without shared context; this skill library gives agents a foundation context file that every marketing skill reads first, then applies task-specific frameworks.
howItWorks: Each skill is a markdown file whose description says when the agent should trigger it, like cro or copywriting.
A product-marketing skill writes a context file covering product, audience and positioning, which every other skill reads before acting.
Skills cross-reference each other, for example copywriting, cro and ab-testing, so related work is chained through a dependency map.
Install with npx skills add, as a Claude Code or Codex plugin, or by copying the skills folder into your agent directory.
The repo ships validation scripts and tests to check skill files, and a guided workflow for read-only first access to marketing accounts.
summary.stealThis: Before your next marketing or non-engineering agent task, write one shared context file (product, audience, positioning) and instruct every skill to read it first, as the product-marketing skill does.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agent skills for non-engineering teams and want a large, real example of skill structure, cross-references and shared context.
summary.quote: The product-marketing skill is the foundation — every other skill checks it first to understand your product, audience, and positioning before doing anything.

verdict.reason: A real, copyable pattern for non-engineering agent work: a foundation product-marketing context file that every skill reads first, plus trigger-style skill descriptions and cross-referenced skills, with dozens of real skill files as evidence; the README itself is mostly catalog and install detail.
